title: Julian Lehr - How to get people excited about your product (Dive Club)
author: Dive Club (Ridd) with Julian Lehr, storytelling lead at Linear
lesson: Linear's in-house creative studio (6 people) treats launch assets as packaging: decide what the product would feel like if you could touch it (robust, aluminium or durable glass, a little friction) and express that through tilted 3D glass assets. Because the real UI is information-dense, the job is 'simplify, simplify, simplify': abstract the complexity and highlight one thing. For an unfinished feature (the Agents beta) they did not explain it but built one signature metaphor ('Hands of God': humans creating AI teammates). Copy, design and motion are developed together in one Figma doc from day one; expect about two weeks of messy exploration before the idea clicks. In layout, spacing is pacing: a gap is a pause.
why: Linear's films are our reference; this is the person who runs Linear's storytelling explaining the reasons behind them (under 20k views, but a top-tier first-hand speaker).

title: The Ultimate Raycast Deep Dive (craft, AI, hype, & more) (Dive Club)
author: Dive Club (Ridd) with Raycast's founders, design team and Hype Team (Pedro Duarte, Inga Hampton)
lesson: Raycast's Hype Team works as an internal mini ad agency: brief, discovery with the product team, exploration, execution. For the iOS launch, discovery fixed the audience (people on the waitlist and existing Mac users), so the film did not sell features: 'beauty is the thing', and visible craft stands for product quality. It is one simple idea (a premium desk setup removed item by item into a box, ending on the phone), shot on 35mm film with music composed for it, about 4 weeks from brainstorm to delivery. The first cut ran 35 s and felt too fast, so they kept a 1:40 'slow burn' because it was for YouTube, not a 45-s ad slot. The Focus ad used one emotional metaphor: chaos, then the light and music change, then a typewriter. They deliberately underhype to manage expectations, and the style changes per feature.
why: A top in-house launch team explains why a slow, single-idea, crafted film beats a feature reel. Only the 'Brand, hype, and identity' chapter (5776-7406 s) is promo-relevant: the episode runs 2 h and has under 20k views.

title: The Launch Video is Dead with Afterimage (LINER NOTES interview)
author: Katie Chiou interviewing Josh Lee (co-founder of Afterimage; led video and production at The Browser Company 2022-2025)
lesson: Repeating the launch-video format everyone has seen, then plugging in your raise, no longer moves the needle. Copying that format reads as 'desperation'; premium reads as 'confidence': a story only this company can tell, with a point of view expressed in the form itself. Messaging and strategy decide the film before any script. Afterimage spends the first 'Ethos Weeks' without discussing video concepts, works in 6-8 week sprints, and refuses to proceed until the team names one P0 audience (for example, customers or investors, not both). Don't take 'one tentpole video' at face value: 3-5 commercials, or one hero plus supporting assets, may serve better.
why: The person behind The Browser Company's films names the premium-vs-average line: original point of view and a single audience, not a borrowed format.

title: Every AI Launch Video Looks the Same Now
author: Damian Player (Doomers)
lesson: It names the 2026 template that marks a film as average: 30-60 s, opening on darkness or a slow reveal, an ambient synth with a rising pad, abstract geometry or particles or a wireframe globe, and dark-mode UI always moving and never held long enough to read. Add one-word text cards cut on the beat, a near-whispered VO, then a resolve to white with the logo and a 'future of' tagline. Viewers recognise the genre in about 2 s and leave. The swap test: replace your end logo with a competitor's; if nothing else in the film becomes untrue, you made a category video. Instead, hold the actual screen long enough to read, show a run that fails and recovers, use a real person in their own register, and show 10 s of real workflow rather than 60 s of atmosphere.
why: It names the red flags of the generic 'cinematic' AI-launch look explicitly, plus a one-line test an agent can run on its own storyboard.

title: Why your launch video looks AI-made, and the tells that give it away
author: LaunchReel
lesson:
It lists seven finish-level tells of a generated or template film, from a frame-by-frame read of about 100 launch videos, each with its premium fix:
1. A fake browser with glossy red/yellow/green dots and a fat URL pill. Fix: small desaturated dots and a dim plain address.
2. A celebratory green checkmark. Fix: resolve the task by brightening a row or flipping a status word from WORKING to DONE.
3. A soft glow behind every dark card. Fix: separate cards by one tonal step plus a 1 px border, and save glow for the logo and end card.
4. Gradient rule lines under headlines.
5. Round placeholder numbers ($12,000, 99%). Fix: jagged real figures ($18,432, 240ms).
6. Body type that scales up with a zoomed card. Fix: keep the type at product size.
7. Ending on the loudest peak. Fix: end on a calm held frame where the logo is still, motion stops and the music resolves.
why: It gives concrete, checkable UI-recreation rules that separate an authored film from a generated one: exactly the details our builders produce.

title: The state of SaaS launch videos in 2026
author: Matt Bingham (Composition, London launch-film studio)
lesson: The hero film's sweet spot moved from 90-120 s two years ago to 40-70 s in 2026. A 60-s film with one job beats a 120-s film with four, and every shot does two jobs. Launch as a system planned on one budget: hero, 2-3 social cuts, a 6-s teaser, a founder follow-up and a site explainer. Show the product, not the product tour: six UI shots in a hero kills it. Use AI for cutdowns, variations and styleframes but never for the hero (audiences spot AI motion within about 3 s). Big VO with soaring music is fading in favour of on-screen type, ambient sound or a real founder voice. Sound design now enters at the storyboard stage, often leaning on one product sound as the hook. A hero with a cut pack takes 4-8 weeks (about 6 typical).
why: A working launch-film studio states current premium norms with numbers (length, deliverable system, VO and sound shift, where AI is acceptable).

title: How We Shaped the Visual Identity for Config 2025
author: Figma Brand Studio (Damien Correll, Chad Colby, Ben Hill, Gilles Desmadrille)
lesson: At Figma, motion starts 'in the front, with everybody on the same level', in parallel with the static identity, not after it locks. The motion team built a motion library and toolkit in Figma (for example, expressive vs functional type treatments) to brief outside partners; Relay animated the opening film. The film's frame rate was dropped from 60 to 15 fps to feel 'tactile and handmade, not so smooth and slick', matching the brand's craft principle even though A/V vendors expected smoothness. Sounds Like These made sonic palettes and motifs used across walk-on music and every product launch video, so the day felt connected: digital-skewed but warm, organic instrumentation. A one-minute ambient 'orchestra warming up' cue replaced the PA announcement.
why: An official in-house account of how a top software brand keeps launch films consistent (one motion library, one sonic palette) and makes a deliberate un-slick choice.

title: Behind the Ship (Vercel Ship 2025 opening film)
author: basement.studio
lesson: Treat a keynote opener like a short film. The pipeline: concept and moodboard (Hackers, Soul and Hey Arnold references, plus visual metaphors for 'prompting reshapes the world'), then full-colour concept art and character design. Next, the animatic is translated into 3D blocking (cameras, scale, a build list), then master keys and poses, then still frames matched to concept art. Full prerender passes come next to retime and add or trim shots; storyboards are not enough. The render goes out as EXR passes with Cryptomatte, followed by a warm grade in Resolve. Everything was animated by hand, pose by pose, with no motion libraries or templates, and 'on twos' (12 fps poses inside 24 fps camera moves) for a graphic, deliberate feel.
why: It shows how Vercel's long-time studio gets a premium tech launch opener: the review gates (animatic, blocking, prerender) and a deliberate frame-rate choice.

title: Stripe Treasury Product Animation (Stripe Sessions 2026)
author: Bartłomiej Otłowski (independent motion designer for Stripe)
lesson: Stripe's own storyboard opened on company registration. They cut that and started 'much closer to the action' (a payment arriving on mobile), then followed one thing (money) through the product instead of listing features. Let the UI explain: large UI close-ups, and buttons that become almost the entire frame, instead of title cards. Real UI is the base; some elements are simplified for animation and kept consistent by a Stripe designer. One recurring device (gradient outlines) guides attention through transitions. The finale rebuilds the full dashboard for the first time. Because the product changed mid-production, values, tables (driven by expressions) and highlights are built as reusable AE rigs. Review ran in Figma for frames, Docs for story and Frame.io in production.
why: A first-hand account of how a Stripe Sessions launch film stages real UI: one subject, close-ups, one attention device, no feature list.

title: Nothing, Playground (launch film case study)
author: BUCK
lesson: For Nothing's AI-tools launch film (script written by Nothing), BUCK avoided product demos and technical detail. It built a flexible design-and-motion system only from the brand's visual DNA (grids, pixels, dots, typography, transparency). One signature move inverted the usual approach: rather than making the tech feel human, they made the human feel technical, weaving footage of people and nature into graphic layers. Contrast pairs carry the look (sharp vectors with organic textures, vibrant gradients over minimal grids). The tone and rhythm came from a large library of styleframes, art-direction studies and motion tests, most of which were cut.
why: It shows how a top studio finds one ownable visual metaphor for an abstract AI feature and keeps every frame inside the brand system.

title: What 149 Tech Videos Reveal About Showcasing the Aha Moment
author: Jai Ghosh (ADVIDS Research)
lesson:
Data from 149 tech product videos (124 companies, Jan-Aug 2026; median runtime 1:11):
- The product appears in 129, at a median 0:12 (78 by 0:15).
- A result (the product visibly producing an output) appears in only 75, at a median 0:34 (48% in). 54 show the product but never show it work, and 20 never show it.
- Videos with a result keep the product on screen 55% of runtime vs 31%, and show it being used first (median 2 segments, 0:20) before it delivers.
- After the result, product shots cover a median 63% of the remaining time.
- 98 of 149 end on a logo card and none on the result; only 27 put an ask or URL in the closing frame.
why: It measures the 'show it working' gap that separates convincing launch films from mood pieces, with timings an agent can plan a timeline against.

title: What 1,000+ SaaS explainer videos have in common (2026 analysis)
author: Rees Gargi (What a Story)
lesson:
Pacing and product-showing distributions from 1,000+ SaaS videos (2015-2026, hand-coded; partly the agency's own library):
- Scene length: 39% change scenes every 3-5 s, 18% every 1-3 s, 26% every 5-7 s.
- Narration: 46% run at 120-140 wpm; above 160 wpm, technical comprehension breaks down.
- UI: 72% show the real product UI, and the most effective show it within the first 15 s. Abstract animation builds interest; real UI builds trust.
- Length: delivered explainers fell from 115 s (2015) to 45 s (2026). 91% of feature-announcement videos stay under 60 s.
- Style: motion graphics 48%, screen capture 27%, live action 15%.
why: It gives baseline shot-length and narration-speed numbers to check a launch animatic against. These are explainer-weighted agency data, so treat them as norms, not the premium ceiling.

title: Wesley Slover - Sound: The Invisible Brand Layer
author: The Booth (Creative Tangent podcast) with Wesley Slover, founder of Sanctus Audio (Discord, Asana sounds)
lesson: Start from what the sound must do (capture attention, reduce friction, build confidence, or sit back), not what it should sound like. Avoid leading with temp tracks, because 'demo love can be really hard to break'. Stock vs custom depends on the story arc: library music holds one mood, so go custom (or customised) when the film has a journey (problem, uncertainty, payoff) or precise musical hits. A great library track is fine when you only need an energy bed. Extend the audio logo into product and UX sounds so marketing and product sound like one brand. Chasing a trendy 'cool' sound can read as unserious and cost credibility.
why: A leading product-sound designer gives a clear rule for the bespoke-score vs licensed-track decision on a launch film. The fetcher returned a partial page, so text_file holds the full text.

title: Creating Sounds That Help Products Thrive
author: Colin Coogan (Antfood)
lesson: The first rule of UX and branded sound is 'Do no harm': a branded cue must never add friction, clutter or make the product feel slower. Reserve expressive brand sounds for infrequent, unambiguously positive moments (Instacart's celebratory sounds). Build energy tiers of the same sound family (Instacart's Mild / Medium / Spicy). Avoid category clichés: for PayPal, Antfood used no coin jingles or cash registers but upward movement, shimmery timbres and tactility ('transaction without transactional'). Context decides everything. Eno's Windows 95 start-up sound shows a sonic logo is 'a tiny little jewel' (that brief asked for 3¼ s).
why: The leading sonic-branding studio gives rules for product UI sounds and sonic logos that a launch film's foley and sting should follow.

title: The Sound of Apple: Tritones, Chords & Origins (Twenty Thousand Hertz, with transcript)
author: Twenty Thousand Hertz with Apple Design Team (Billy Sorrentino, Hugo Verweij) and Kelly Jacklin
lesson: At Apple, sound 'is at the beginning of the design process. It isn't a coat of paint at the end'. Sound designers sit at the table with industrial, 3D, interaction and haptics designers from the first product ideas. Inspiration is the product itself: hardware, materials, how it feels in the hand, then the UI animations, UI colours and haptics. Apple records real instruments (glockenspiel, kalimba) for organic, familiar timbres that make new technology feel comfortable. It builds a palette of about five processed 'instruments' from recordings (reversed, filtered, reverbed) and composes each sound from that palette.
why: It explains, first-hand from Apple's design team, how premium product sound is derived from the object and its UI motion. That is the basis for UI foley in our launch films.

title: Motion Graphics Production Workflow: Brief to Delivery
author: Art of Styleframe Editorial
lesson:
Eight gated stages for a 60-90 s piece, 5-7 weeks in total:
- Brief: 3-5 days. Names one audience, one message, duration and deliverables, signed by a named decision maker.
- Script and boards: 4-6 days.
- Styleframes: 3-5 days, about a week for 3D. 2-3 frames at delivery resolution, each with a note on what will move.
- Animatic: 2-3 days. Burnt-in timecode; locks shot durations.
- Animation: 10-15 days.
- Sound and mix: 3-4 days, only after picture lock.
- Review rounds: about 5 days budgeted across stages.
- Delivery: 1-2 days.
Each stage gets two review rounds (round 2 is polish only), and each gate locks a layer: brief/scope, script/words, boards/structure, styleframes/look, animatic/timing, picture lock/motion, mix/everything. Feedback against a locked layer is a change request. Use a frame-accurate review tool, not emailed timestamps.
why: It gives explicit approval gates and durations for our agent pipeline (storyboard, styleframe, animatic, picture lock, mix). It is one practitioner's model; its 'change requests tripled' figure is an anecdote, not a study.

title: Sound in Motion: A PODCAST with Sono Sanctus (full transcript)
author: School of Motion (Joey Korenman) with Wesley Slover and Trevor Richardson of Sono Sanctus
lesson:
It describes the sound process for a designed motion piece, step by step:
- Start with the music first, because it shapes everything.
- Lay several library tracks against the cut and ask what the client likes and dislikes, which yields a tempo range.
- Then sound-design a ~15-second demo section and treat it like a style frame to agree the palette.
- Build a project-specific sound library that is harmonious with the music.
- Sync sounds to on-screen events (a piece with nothing happening on screen gives sound nothing to anchor to).
- In the final mix, remove more than you add to leave room for the sound design.
why: It is still the canonical case-study breakdown (2019) of how a top motion-graphics sound studio scores a short brand piece; it gives agents a music-first, demo-section workflow.
